claims.evidence: This is based on the HDX-MS data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: S828 is the only site capable of CK1α-mediated phosphorylation without previous priming phosphorylation.
claims.source: We observed phosphorylation of the 828o mutant, but not of any of the other four (Figure 5a). Thus, only S828 can get phosphorylated by CK1α in vitro in the absence of prior priming phosphorylation.
claims.evidence: This is directly measured in the in vitro phosphorylation assays with 'single open' mutants shown in Figure 5a.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation was not impacted when acidic residues proposed to provide a non-primed canonical recognition sequence were mutated to neutral ones.
claims.source: An upstream acidic cluster in the EI was proposed to provide a non-primed canonical recognition sequence (Golden et al., 2017) however, we found that phosphorylation was not impacted when we mutated those acidic residues to neutral ones (i.e. E821Q/D823N/E826Q) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured in the in vitro phosphorylation assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: pS828 is capable of priming for phosphorylation of S831.
claims.source: The 'double o' mutant in which S828 and S831 were open (i.e. Ago2(T830A, S831A, S834A)) showed significantly increased phosphorylation, whereas the mutants with 824, 830, or 834 open showed only minor increases (Figure 5b). This suggested that pS828 is capable of priming for phosphorylation of S831.
claims.evidence: This is directly measured in the in vitro phosphorylation assays with 'double open' mutants shown in Figure 5b.

claims.claim: After the second phosphorylation at S831, the EI phosphorylation pattern can follow different routes and is more heterogenous.
claims.source: We saw an increase in phosphorylation in all three cases, suggesting that, after the second phosphorylation at S831, the EI phosphorylation pattern can follow different routes and is more heterogenous than the initial S828 followed by S831 phosphorylation pattern (Figure 5c).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured in the in vitro phosphorylation assays with 'triple open' mutants shown in Figure 5c.

claims.claim: Mutation of S828 to alanine prevented almost all detectable phosphorylation.
claims.source: Importantly, mutation of S828 to alanine prevented almost all detectable phosphorylation and mutation of S831 to alanine substantially decreased phosphorylalation (Figure 5d), supporting their key roles in the hierarchy of EI phosphorylation.
claims.evidence: This is directly measured in the in vitro phosphorylation assays shown in Figure 5d.

claims.claim: CK1α-mediated phosphorylation of wt hAgo2 significantly increased koff by ~7.5-fold.
claims.source: CK1α-mediated phosphorylation of wt hAgo2 significantly increased koff by ~7.5-fold, and thus decreased the half-life of the RISC/target complex (Figure 6a).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured in the target release assays shown in Figure 6a.

claims.claim: CK1α-mediated treatment of hAgo2(5XA) had no effect on target release.
claims.source: These effects are specific to EI phosphorylation, as CK1α-mediated treatment of hAgo2(5XA) had no effect.
claims.evidence: This is directly measured in the target release assays shown in Figure 6a.

claims.claim: The effects of phosphorylation on target release are additive – the more sites available for phosphorylation, the larger the observed effect.
claims.source: These effects are additive – the more sites available for phosphorylation, the larger the observed effect (828o < 828o;831o < 828o;831o;834o) (Figure 6b).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured in the target release assays shown in Figure 6b.

claims.claim: Under high salt conditions, differences between the off-rate of CK1α-treated and untreated wt hAgo2 were much smaller, only ~1.5-fold higher for phosphorylated hAgo2.
claims.source: In these conditions, differences between the off-rate of CK1α-treated and untreated wt hAgo2 were much smaller, only ~1.5-fold higher for phosphorylated hAgo2, supporting the hypothesis that the effects of phosphorylation on promoting target release are largely electrostatically mediated (Figure 6c).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured in the target release assays under high salt conditions shown in Figure 6c.

claims.claim: The effects of phosphorylation on promoting target release are largely electrostatically mediated.
claims.source: In these conditions, differences between the off-rate of CK1α-treated and untreated wt hAgo2 were much smaller, only ~1.5-fold higher for phosphorylated hAgo2, supporting the hypothesis that the effects of phosphorylation on promoting target release are largely electrostatically mediated (Figure 6c).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of target release under normal and high salt conditions shown in Figure 6c.

claims.claim: Each miRNA family typically has hundreds of targets.
claims.source: Each miRNA family, in turn, typically has hundreds of targets; the 90 most broadly conserved miRNA families have over 400 conserved targets each (Friedman et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Friedman et al., 2009.

claims.claim: The number of miRNA target sites is much greater than the number of miRNA-Ago complexes.
claims.source: At the same time, the number of miRNA target sites is much greater than the number of miRNA-Ago complexes (Denzler et al., 2014) and the half-lives of mRNAs are, on average, significantly shorter than those of RISC complexes (Kingston and Bartel, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Denzler et al., 2014 and Kingston and Bartel, 2019.

claims.claim: Each core RISC targets multiple mRNAs throughout its lifetime.
claims.source: Therefore, it appears that each core RISC targets multiple mRNAs throughout its lifetime.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data about target site excess and RISC stability.

claims.claim: Repression efficacy is largely related to binding stability, with stronger binding correlating with enhanced repression.
claims.source: On the other hand, repression efficacy is largely related to binding stability, with stronger binding correlating with enhanced repression (McGeary et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to McGeary et al., 2019.

claims.claim: CK1α-mediated EI phosphorylation provides a mechanism to counterbalance the added affinity from 3' supplementary pairing, freeing RISC to repress additional targets.
claims.source: 3' supplementary pairing increases binding affinity and thus can lead to enhanced repression at cognate sites (Becker et al., 2019), but high affinity may come with the risk of effectively sequestering RISC. CK1α-mediated EI phosphorylation provides a mechanism to counterbalance this added affinity, freeing RISC to repress additional targets.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and represents the main mechanistic interpretation of the study.

claims.claim: In vitro, 3' supplementary pairing can significantly enhance the stability of Ago/target interactions, with 3–4 contiguous canonical base pairs in the supplementary region increasing affinity over 20-fold for some miRNA/target pairs.
claims.source: In vitro, 3' supplementary pairing can significantly enhance the stability of Ago/target interactions, with 3–4 contiguous canonical base pairs in the supplementary region increasing affinity over 20-fold for some miRNA/target pairs (Sheu-Gruttadauria et al., 2019b; Xiao and MacRae, 2020; Salomon et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Sheu-Gruttadauria et al., 2019b, Xiao and MacRae, 2020, and Salomon et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The contributions of supplementary pairing in vivo and in cell culture are less substantial than in vitro.
claims.source: However, several reports concluded that the contributions of supplementary pairing in vivo and in cell culture are less substantial (Grimson et al., 2007; Wee et al., 2012; Salomon et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Grimson et al., 2007, Wee et al., 2012, and Salomon et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Supplementary pairing triggers phosphorylation of the EI, which could offset added binding affinity, explaining why the overall effects of supplementary pairing on target repression appear less pronounced in vivo.
claims.source: However, as we have shown in this study, supplementary pairing triggers phosphorylation of the EI, which could offset added binding affinity. Therefore, in vivo, the overall effects of supplementary pairing on target repression would appear to be less pronounced.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and represents an interpretation of the study's findings.

claims.claim: CK1α phosphorylation likely occurs in a distributive manner.
claims.source: CK1α phosphorylation likely occurs in a distributive manner (Gebel et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gebel et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Target retention time is not the primary driver of CK1α-mediated EI phosphorylation.
claims.source: However, we found that target retention time is not the primary driver of CK1α-mediated EI phosphorylation, as demonstrated by the minimal levels of phosphorylation observed upon binding to the fully complementary or TDMD-like target.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data shown in Figure 2b comparing different target types.

claims.claim: The conformation of the RISC complex is of primary importance with regard to triggering phosphorylation.
claims.source: Our findings instead suggest that the conformation of the RISC complex is of primary importance with regard to triggering phosphorylation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data showing differential phosphorylation with different target complementarity patterns.

claims.claim: A variety of germline single amino acid mutations in hAgo2 were linked to RNAi deficits and neurological symptoms.
claims.source: Recently, a study linked a variety of germline single amino acid mutations in hAgo2 to RNAi deficits and neurological symptoms (Lessel et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lessel et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Some of the mutated Agos had decreased EI phosphorylation and a slight increase in quantity of select target mRNAs when expressed in cell culture.
claims.source: These mutations clustered in helix 7, L1, and a loop in the PIWI domain, and, when expressed in cell culture, some of the mutated Agos had decreased EI phosphorylation and a slight increase in quantity of select target mRNAs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lessel et al., 2020 in the preceding context.

claims.claim: Substrate tertiary structure has been shown to be critical for promoting CK1-mediated phosphorylation in multiple examples.
claims.source: There are multiple examples in the literature where substrate tertiary structure has been shown to be critical for promoting CK1-mediated phosphorylation. For example, T-antigen is phosphorylated by CK1 at non-canonical sites at its N-terminus in a manner that is dependent on proper folding and an intact C-terminus (Cegielska et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cegielska et al., 1994.

claims.claim: The EI shows no significant changes in deuterium exchange upon guide- or target-binding.
claims.source: Since the EI shows no significant changes in deuterium exchange neither upon guide- nor upon target-binding, the additional information needed to enable phosphorylation stems from outside of the EI.
claims.evidence: This is based on the HDX-MS data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The target RNA's backbone, being negatively charged, may be able to bind to the kinase's Anion Binding Site 1 and prime for S828 phosphorylation.
claims.source: We would like to suggest that it is the target RNA's backbone, being negatively charged, that may be able to bind to this site and prime for S828 phosphorylation.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain the mechanism of phosphorylation.

claims.claim: An unphosphorylated EI peptide could not be phosphorylated by recombinant CK1α.
claims.source: Golden et al. reported that an unphosphorylated EI peptide could not be phosphorylated by recombinant CK1α, leading them to propose that contextual features in the full-length hAgo2 were required in order to make S828 a suitable CK1α substrate.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Golden et al., 2017 in the preceding context.

claims.claim: It is not only full-length hAgo2 that is required for phosphorylation, but rather hAgo2 bound to a guide and target RNA with seed and supplementary region pairing.
claims.source: Our work shows that it is not only full-length hAgo2 that is required, but rather hAgo2 bound to a guide and target RNA with seed and supplementary region pairing.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing target-dependent phosphorylation.

claims.claim: S828A mutation eliminated detectable phosphorylation of hAgo2 in HCT116 cells lacking expression of ANKRD52.
claims.source: This was further supported by their finding that S828A mutation, but not a single A mutation at any of the other phosphorylatable residues in the EI, eliminated detectable phosphorylation of hAgo2 in HCT116 cells lacking expression of ANKRD52, a regulatory subunit of PP6 (Golden et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Golden et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Mutating the corresponding serine to S828 in C. elegans hAgo2 homolog ALG-1 (S992) to alanine led to severe developmental defects similar to those seen when mutating all EI phosphorylation sites to alanine.
claims.source: Huberdeau et al. found that mutating the corresponding serine in the C. elegans hAgo2 homolog ALG-1 (S992) to alanine led to severe developmental defects similar to those seen when mutating all EI phosphorylation sites to alanine (Quévillon Huberdeau et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Quévillon Huberdeau et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Expression of hAgo2(S828A), but not wt hAgo2, was able to rescue repression of a miR-19 EGFP reporter in ANKRD52-deficient cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, Golden et al. reported that expression of hAgo2(S828A), but not wt hAgo2, was able to rescue repression of a miR-19 EGFP reporter in ANKRD52-deficient cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Golden et al., 2017 in the preceding context.

claims.claim: EI phosphorylation does not impact hAgo2/GW182 interaction.
claims.source: Previous studies have found that EI phosphorylation does not impact hAgo2/GW182 interaction (Golden et al., 2017; Quévillon Huberdeau et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Golden et al., 2017 and Quévillon Huberdeau et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation is not required for CK1α-mediated phosphorylation of Ago, as it can be observed in the absence of additional proteins.
claims.source: However, since we are able to observe Ago phosphorylation in the absence of additional proteins, they are not required for CKα-mediated phosphorylation.
claims.evidence: This is based on the in vitro phosphorylation assays performed with recombinant proteins.

claims.claim: Knocking out PP6 in human cell lines led to a global decrease in RISC binding to mRNA.
claims.source: Knocking out PP6 in human cell lines led to a global decrease in RISC binding to mRNA (Golden et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Golden et al., 2017.

claims.claim: CK1α-mediated EI phosphorylation is rapidly countered by dephosphorylation under normal conditions.
claims.source: Under normal conditions, however, CK1α-mediated EI phosphorylation is rapidly countered by dephosphorylation (Golden et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Golden et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Neither 5XA nor 5XE hAgo2 could rescue miRNA-mediated repression in Ago2-/- cells, indicating that the phosphorylation cycling process itself is important.
claims.source: Despite this, neither 5XA nor 5XE hAgo2 could rescue miRNA-mediated repression in Ago2-/- cells, indicating that the phosphorylation cycling process itself is important, not merely the presence or absence of phosphorylation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies in the context.

claims.claim: Target binding serves as a means for regulating CK1α-mediated phosphorylation of Ago, which, in turn, regulates RISC turnover and thus miRNA-mediated mRNA repression.
claims.source: We therefore propose that target binding serves as a means for regulating CK1α-mediated phosphorylation of Ago, which, in turn, regulates RISC turnover and thus miRNA-mediated mRNA repression.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, synthesizing all the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation, or at least phosphorylation of enough sites to efficiently promote target release, happens after target repression is established.
claims.source: However, given the previous in vivo findings showing widespread regulatory defects with both hyper- and hypophosphorylation (Golden et al., 2017; Quévillon Huberdeau et al., 2017), we speculate that phosphorylation, or at least phosphorylation of enough sites to efficiently promote target release, happens after target repression is established.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors based on previous findings.

claims.claim: The requirement for multiple phosphorylations could help ensure that there is enough time for the initiation of repression to occur before the target is released.
claims.source: The requirement for multiple phosphorylations could help ensure that there is enough time for the initiation of repression to occur before the target is released.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claims.claim: Direct tethering of GW182 family proteins to mRNA can bypass the need for RISC.
claims.source: Direct tethering of GW182 family proteins to mRNA can bypass the need for RISC (Behm-Ansmant et al., 2006; Zipprich et al., 2009), suggesting that if enough Ago-independent interactions between repressive machinery and the mRNA are formed, Ago may even be able to be released while repression is ongoing.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Behm-Ansmant et al., 2006 and Zipprich et al., 2009.

claims.claim: This mechanism appears specialized for repression mediated by miRNA, as opposed to siRNA, as binding to fully complementary sites only triggers minimal phosphorylation.
claims.source: This mechanism appears specialized for repression mediated by miRNA, as opposed to siRNA, as binding to fully complementary sites only triggers minimal phosphorylation (Figure 2b) and phosphomimicking does not impair slicing (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on the data shown in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: With siRNA, slicing of the fully complementary target promotes its release by destabilizing the guide/target duplex.
claims.source: With siRNA, slicing of the fully complementary target promotes its release by destabilizing the guide/target duplex (Salomon et al., 2015), but partially-complementary miRNAs with high affinity, such as those with 3' supplementary pairing, could get stuck on a target and phosphorylation could serve as a mechanism to promote their release in the absence of slicing.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Salomon et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Extending 3' pairing in the absence of central pairing decreased EI phosphorylation.
claims.source: However, we found that extending 3' pairing in the absence of central pairing also decreased EI phosphorylation (Figure 2b).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured in the in vitro phosphorylation assays shown in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: Targets with extended 3' pairing can induce TDMD in vivo, which resolves the interaction through degradation of the RISC complex.
claims.source: Such targets can induce TDMD in vivo, which resolves the interaction through degradation of the RISC complex (Shi et al., 2020; Han et al., 2020), and therefore these targets would not need phosphorylation-promoted release to resolve RISC/target interactions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Shi et al., 2020 and Han et al., 2020.

claims.claim: This regulatory mechanism is likely shared by miRNA-handling Ago orthologs hAgo1, hAgo2, and hAgo3.
claims.source: Therefore, this regulatory mechanism is likely shared by these miRNA-handling Ago orthologs, suggesting a potentially broad impact on post-transcriptional regulation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that hAgo1 and hAgo3 also undergo target-triggered phosphorylation.

claims.claim: Ago EI phosphorylation is a post-target-binding regulatory mechanism that promotes target release, freeing guide-bound Ago from the mRNA target.
claims.source: In conclusion, our findings show that Ago EI phosphorylation is a post-target-binding regulatory mechanism that promotes target release, freeing guide-bound Ago, namely RISC, from the mRNA target and dissuading it from binding more targets until it gets dephosphorylated by PPP6C/ANKRD52 (Golden et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, synthesizing all the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Dephosphorylation by PPP6C/ANKRD52 was previously shown to be rapid.
claims.source: This dephosphorylation was previously shown to be rapid (Golden et al., 2017), therefore the released Ago-guide complex is likely to quickly be able to seek out and repress additional targets.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Golden et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The phosphorylation/dephosphorylation cycle allows cells to strike a balance between the increased efficacy and specificity provided by stronger binding sites and the quest for efficiency, allowing a single miRISC to repress multiple mRNAs.
claims.source: As long as the cycle of phosphorylation/dephosphorylation is not disrupted, this would allow cells to strike a balance between the increased efficacy and specificity provided by stronger binding sites and the quest for efficiency, allowing a single miRISC to repress multiple mRNAs (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is the main mechanistic interpretation and conclusion of the study, illustrated in Figure 7.

claims.claim: This mechanism of promoting miRNA target release appears specialized for miRNA-mediated repression.
claims.source: This mechanism of promoting miRNA target release appears specialized for miRNA-mediated repression and the broad conservation of the phosphorylation sites suggests that its use is widespread among miRNA-handling Ago proteins.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the conservation data and the specificity of the mechanism for miRNA targets.

claims.claim: The broad conservation of the phosphorylation sites suggests that the use of this mechanism is widespread among miRNA-handling Ago proteins.
claims.source: This mechanism of promoting miRNA target release appears specialized for miRNA-mediated repression and the broad conservation of the phosphorylation sites suggests that its use is widespread among miRNA-handling Ago proteins.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the conservation analysis shown in Figure 1a.

claims.claim: The EI is absent in prokaryotic Ago proteins.
claims.source: As noted above, EI is a feature that is characteristic of eukaryotic miRNA-specialized Ago proteins and is absent in prokaryotic Ago proteins.
claims.evidence: This is shown in the conservation analysis in Figure 1a.

claims.claim: The EI is absent in siRNA- or piRNA-specialized Ago superfamily proteins.
claims.source: We noticed that it is also absent in siRNA- or piRNA-specialized Ago superfamily proteins (e.g. Drosophila melanogaster Ago2 and Piwi proteins, respectively) (Figure 1a).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the conservation analysis in Figure 1a.

claims.claim: ZT1 corresponds to a natural, highly conserved, miR-200-binding site in the 3' UTR of the transcription factor ZEB1.
claims.source: For this target, we used a 30-nt RNA we will refer to as ZT1, which corresponds to a natural, highly conserved, miR-200-binding site in the 3' UTR of the transcription factor ZEB1 (Gregory et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gregory et al., 2008.

claims.claim: The ZT1 target's genomic location was identified as bound to 5XA but not wild-type hAgo2 in previous eCLIP experiments.
claims.source: This guide/target combination was chosen because the target's genomic location was identified as bound to 5XA but not wild-type (wt) hAgo2 in previous eCLIP experiments (Golden et al., 2017), suggesting it was sensitive to EI phosphorylation in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Golden et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The miR-200/ZT1 pair is functionally relevant in helping regulate epithelial to mesenchymal transitions.
claims.source: It was also chosen because of its functional relevance in helping regulate epithelial to mesenchymal transitions (Gregory et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gregory et al., 2008.

claims.claim: 14 nt represents the shortest length of target capable of establishing stable pairing in the supplementary region.
claims.source: It is likely that 14 nt represents the shortest length of target capable of establishing stable pairing in the supplementary region.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that 14 nt is the minimum length for robust phosphorylation.

claims.claim: EI phosphomimetics do not significantly affect slicing.
claims.source: This result is consistent with our finding that EI phosphomimetics do not significantly affect slicing (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured in the slicer assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The 5XA mutant has a similar target-binding affinity compared to dephosphorylated wt hAgo2.
claims.source: Since no reliable peptides covering the EI could be measured for wt hAgo2, we used the 5XA mutant, which has a similar target-binding affinity compared to dephosphorylated wt (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), yet did have reliable coverage of the EI.
claims.evidence: This is directly measured in the filter-binding assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The 5XA mutant showed minimal differences in exchange compared to the dephosphorylated wt RNA-free hAgo2 over the rest of the protein.
claims.source: The 5XA mutant showed minimal differences in exchange compared to the dephosphorylated wt RNA-free hAgo2 over the rest of the protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on the HDX-MS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Near-complete (99.4%) sequence coverage was achieved in the HDX-MS experiments, with a total of 262 peptides and an average redundancy of 5.29.
claims.source: Near-complete (99.4%) sequence coverage was achieved, with a total of 262 peptides and an average redundancy of 5.29 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a technical detail about the HDX-MS experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The RNA-free state showed higher relative uptake over most of the protein compared to guide-bound, suggesting greater overall flexibility prior to guide binding.
claims.source: However, the RF also showed higher relative uptake over most of the protein, suggesting greater overall flexibility prior to guide binding.
claims.evidence: This is based on the HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Guide binding protects hAgo2 from limited proteolysis.
claims.source: This is consistent with previous results showing guide binding protects from limited proteolysis (Elkayam et al., 2012) and with the observation that RNA-free hAgo2 is unstable in cells and rapidly degraded (Martinez and Gregory, 2013), whereas G-bound hAgo2 complexes are incredibly stable (Olejniczak et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Elkayam et al., 2012, Martinez and Gregory, 2013, and Olejniczak et al., 2013.

claims.claim: RNA-free hAgo2 is unstable in cells and rapidly degraded.
claims.source: This is consistent with previous results showing guide binding protects from limited proteolysis (Elkayam et al., 2012) and with the observation that RNA-free hAgo2 is unstable in cells and rapidly degraded (Martinez and Gregory, 2013), whereas G-bound hAgo2 complexes are incredibly stable (Olejniczak et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Martinez and Gregory, 2013.

claims.claim: G-bound hAgo2 complexes are incredibly stable.
claims.source: This is consistent with previous results showing guide binding protects from limited proteolysis (Elkayam et al., 2012) and with the observation that RNA-free hAgo2 is unstable in cells and rapidly degraded (Martinez and Gregory, 2013), whereas G-bound hAgo2 complexes are incredibly stable (Olejniczak et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Olejniczak et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Differences between the G-bound and GT-bound states in HDX-MS were localized mainly to regions expected based on crystal structures, including the L1 linker and helix 7 of the L2 linker region.
claims.source: Differences between the G-bound and GT-bound states were more subtle. Significant differences were localized mainly to regions expected based on crystal structures, including the L1 linker and helix 7 of the L2 linker region (Figure 4), which undergo a rigid body movement upon target binding, widening the N-PAZ channel to accommodate pairing beyond the seed sequence (Schirle et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is based on the HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4 and supported by a citation to Schirle et al., 2014.

claims.claim: CK1α has a canonical sequence preference of pS/pT-x-x-S/T* or (E,D)n-x-x-S/T*-x.
claims.source: CK1α has a canonical sequence preference of pS/pT-x-x-S/T* or (E,D)n-x-x-S/T*-x where 'p' indicates a phosphorylated site, * indicates the site to be phosphorylated, and 'x' indicates any amino acid (Venerando et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Venerando et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Prior phosphorylation can prime for subsequent phosphorylation by CK1α, making CK1α capable of hierarchical phosphorylation.
claims.source: Thus, prior phosphorylation (by CK1α or another kinase) can prime for subsequent phosphorylation, making CK1α capable of hierarchical phosphorylation. This has been proposed to occur at the EI (Golden et al., 2017), however heterogeneity has hindered past attempts to characterize EI phosphorylation status at the amino acid level.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Golden et al., 2017 and represents established knowledge about CK1α.

claims.claim: An S828 phosphomimetic (S828E) failed to prime for further phosphorylation.
claims.source: We first tried an S828 phosphomimetic (S828E). This failed to prime for further phosphorylation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), however glutamate is different in size and charge to phosphoserine and thus may not sufficiently recapitulate the effects of true phosphorylation (Chen and Cole, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured in the in vitro phosphorylation assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Glutamate may not sufficiently recapitulate the effects of true phosphorylation.
claims.source: This failed to prime for further phosphorylation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), however glutamate is different in size and charge to phosphoserine and thus may not sufficiently recapitulate the effects of true phosphorylation (Chen and Cole, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chen and Cole, 2015.

claims.claim: The overall charge, rather than the specific phosphorylated sites, is most important for target release.
claims.source: The 'triple o' mutant 824o;828o;831o showed similar effects as 828o;831o;834o (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the overall charge, rather than the specific phosphorylated sites, is most important for target release.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the target release assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Binding of the phosphorylated priming residue or a cluster of acidic residues to Anion Binding Site 1 on CK1 is thought to stabilize the kinase in an active conformation and position the downstream phosphorylation site in the active site.
claims.source: Binding of the phosphorylated, priming residue, or a cluster of acidic residues to a basic patch on the kinase, named Anion Binding Site 1, is thought to stabilize the kinase in an active conformation and position the downstream phosphorylation site in the active site (Gebel et al., 2020; Philpott et al., 2020; Longenecker et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Gebel et al., 2020, Philpott et al., 2020, and Longenecker et al., 1996.

claims.claim: The need for seed + supplementary pairing supports a role for conformational change in positioning the RNA to interact with the kinase properly.
claims.source: The need for seed + supplementary pairing as opposed to other complementarity combinations in order to trigger robust phosphorylation supports a role for conformational change. These changes might position the RNA to interact with the kinase properly, rather than making the EI more accessible.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data showing specificity for seed + supplementary pairing.

claims.claim: Peptides phosphorylated at S828 were able to be phosphorylated at S831 and those phosphorylated at S831 were able to be phosphorylated at S834.
claims.source: Golden et al. showed that peptides phosphorylated at S828 were able to be phosphorylated at S831 and those phosphorylated at S831 were able to be phosphorylated at S834.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Golden et al., 2017 in the preceding context.

results.result: Target binding alone stimulates CK1α-mediated phosphorylation of hAgo2 in vitro. RNA-free and guide-only hAgo2 showed minimal phosphorylation (0.14 ± 0.07 mol/mol), while guide+target hAgo2 showed substantial phosphorylation (2.6 ± 0.2 mol/mol). The 5XA mutant showed no phosphorylation, confirming EI-dependence.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C36 provide direct experimental evidence from in vitro phosphorylation assays (Figure 1c) with appropriate controls including RNA-free, guide-only, and 5XA mutant conditions. The quantitative measurements with error bars support the conclusion that target binding is necessary and sufficient for phosphorylation.

results.result: hAgo1 and hAgo3 also undergo target-binding-triggered CK1α-mediated phosphorylation in vitro, suggesting this regulatory mechanism is shared among miRNA-handling Ago orthologs.
results.evaluation: Claims C37 and C89 are supported by direct experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1. The extension to other Ago orthologs strengthens the generalizability of the mechanism, though the functional consequences were not tested for hAgo1/3.

results.result: A minimum of 14 nucleotides of target RNA is required to trigger robust phosphorylation, likely representing the shortest length capable of establishing stable pairing in the supplementary region.
results.evaluation: Claim C38 is directly supported by experimental data in Figure 2a showing dramatic increase in phosphorylation at 14 nt. Claim C100 provides a reasonable mechanistic interpretation. The binding affinity data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) rules out affinity differences as the explanation.

results.result: Seed + supplementary pairing configuration specifically triggers phosphorylation. Seed-only, fully complementary, and extended 3' complementarity targets all failed to trigger robust phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C42 are supported by systematic testing of different target complementarity patterns in Figure 2b. The use of catalytically dead hAgo2 as a control for the fully complementary target strengthens the conclusion. The specificity for seed + supplementary pairing is a key mechanistic insight.

results.result: HDX-MS analysis shows the EI has high deuterium exchange with no significant changes upon guide or target binding, indicating the EI remains flexible and solvent-accessible in all states, and that neither guide nor target binding offers protection to phosphorylatable residues.
results.evaluation: Claims C43, C44, and C69 are supported by HDX-MS data in Figure 3. The use of 5XA mutant as a proxy for wt is justified by binding affinity and HDX comparison data (Figure 3—figure supplements 1-2). The conclusion that conformational information comes from outside the EI is logical.

results.result: S828 is the only EI residue capable of CK1α-mediated phosphorylation without prior priming. Mutation of S828 to alanine prevents almost all detectable phosphorylation, and the previously proposed acidic cluster does not serve as a priming sequence.
results.evaluation: Claims C45, C46, and C49 are supported by systematic mutagenesis experiments in Figure 5a, 5d, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1. The 'single open' mutant approach is elegant and provides clear evidence for S828 as the initiating site. The negative result with acidic cluster mutations refutes a prior hypothesis.

results.result: EI phosphorylation occurs hierarchically: pS828 primes for S831 phosphorylation, and after pS831, phosphorylation becomes more heterogeneous with multiple possible third/fourth sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C47 and C48 are supported by 'double open' and 'triple open' mutant experiments in Figure 5b-c. The systematic approach clearly demonstrates the hierarchical nature of phosphorylation. The heterogeneity after S831 is well-documented by the triple open mutant data.

results.result: CK1α-mediated phosphorylation increases target release rate by ~7.5-fold in wt hAgo2 but has no effect on 5XA mutant. The effect is additive with more phosphorylation sites producing larger effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C52 are supported by target release assays in Figure 6a-b with appropriate controls and quantification. The use of 5XA as a negative control and the dose-response with 1, 2, and 3 open sites provide strong evidence for the functional consequence of phosphorylation.

results.result: The effect of phosphorylation on target release is largely electrostatically mediated. Under high salt conditions, the difference between phosphorylated and unphosphorylated hAgo2 is reduced from ~7.5-fold to ~1.5-fold, and overall charge rather than specific sites is most important.
results.evaluation: Claims C53, C54, and C114 are supported by high salt experiments in Figure 6c and Figure 6—figure supplement 1. The electrostatic shielding experiment is a strong mechanistic test. The comparison of different triple open mutants supports the charge-based model.

results.result: Target binding with seed + supplementary pairing triggers hierarchical EI phosphorylation by CK1α, which electrostatically promotes target release, allowing RISC to balance binding affinity with turnover efficiency for repressing multiple targets.
results.evaluation: These claims represent the main conclusions synthesizing all experimental findings. They are well-supported by the combined evidence from phosphorylation assays (Figures 1-2, 5), HDX-MS (Figures 3-4), and target release assays (Figure 6). The model in Figure 7 integrates the findings coherently.

results.result: The study provides a mechanistic explanation for why 3' supplementary pairing has less pronounced effects in vivo than in vitro: supplementary pairing triggers EI phosphorylation, which offsets the added binding affinity.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 integrate prior literature (citations provided) with the current findings. The explanation is logical and supported by the data showing that seed + supplementary targets specifically trigger phosphorylation. This reconciles an apparent discrepancy in the field.

results.result: RISC conformation, rather than target retention time, is the primary driver of phosphorylation. The need for seed + supplementary pairing supports a role for conformational change in positioning RNA to interact with the kinase.
results.evaluation: Claims C64, C65, and C116 are supported by the differential phosphorylation observed with different target types (Figure 2b). The minimal phosphorylation of fully complementary and TDMD-like targets, despite their expected longer retention times, strongly supports this conclusion.

results.result: The authors propose that the target RNA backbone may bind to CK1α's Anion Binding Site 1 to prime for S828 phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claim C70 is explicitly speculative and not directly tested. While the hypothesis is reasonable given the non-canonical nature of S828 phosphorylation and the failure of acidic cluster mutations, it requires experimental validation such as kinase-RNA interaction studies or structural analysis.

results.result: The 5XA mutant is validated as an appropriate proxy for dephosphorylated wt hAgo2 in HDX-MS experiments, showing similar target-binding affinity and minimal differences in deuterium exchange over the rest of the protein, with 99.4% sequence coverage achieved.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C104 are supported by control experiments in Figure 3—figure supplements 1-3. The validation of 5XA as a proxy is important for interpreting the HDX-MS results, and the high sequence coverage indicates good data quality.

results.result: EI phosphomimetics do not significantly affect slicing activity, and the phosphorylation mechanism appears specialized for miRNA-mediated repression rather than siRNA function.
results.evaluation: Claims C101 and C85 are supported by slicer assays in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and the differential phosphorylation data in Figure 2b. The conservation analysis (Figure 1a) showing EI absence in siRNA-specialized Agos further supports this conclusion.

results.result: HDX-MS reveals that RNA-free hAgo2 is more flexible overall than guide-bound, and target binding causes conformational changes localized to L1 linker and helix 7 of L2 linker, consistent with known structural changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C109 are supported by HDX-MS data in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, with appropriate citations to structural studies. These findings validate the HDX-MS approach and provide context for understanding why the EI itself doesn't change.

results.result: An S828E phosphomimetic failed to prime for further phosphorylation, possibly because glutamate does not sufficiently recapitulate true phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C112 and C113 are supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and a citation explaining limitations of phosphomimetics. This negative result is important for understanding why the 'open' mutant strategy was necessary.

results.result: The high conservation of EI phosphosites in eukaryotic miRNA-specialized Ago proteins, but absence in prokaryotic and siRNA/piRNA-specialized Agos, suggests this regulatory mechanism is widespread among miRNA-handling Ago proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C93-C96 are supported by the conservation analysis in Figure 1a. The evolutionary pattern strongly suggests functional importance, though the inference about widespread use requires the assumption that conservation implies function.

results.result: Background on RNAi mechanism, Ago protein structure and function, miRNA targeting rules, and human Ago orthologs.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1-C25) provide established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations. They set the context for the study but do not represent novel findings.

results.result: Prior work established that CK1α phosphorylates the EI cluster, affecting target association and miRNA-mediated repression, but the mechanism was undetermined.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C26-C32 accurately summarize prior work with appropriate citations. They establish the knowledge gap that this study addresses.

results.result: Each miRNA family has hundreds of targets, target sites greatly outnumber RISC complexes, and each RISC likely targets multiple mRNAs, creating a need to balance binding stability with turnover.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58 are supported by appropriate citations and provide important context for why the phosphorylation mechanism is functionally significant.

results.result: Background on CK1α phosphorylation mechanisms, including canonical sequence preferences, hierarchical phosphorylation capability, and the role of Anion Binding Site 1.
results.evaluation: Claims C63, C110, C111, and C115 provide established knowledge about CK1α with appropriate citations, contextualizing the non-canonical phosphorylation observed in this study.

results.result: Prior studies linked hAgo2 mutations to RNAi deficits and showed that substrate tertiary structure can be critical for CK1-mediated phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 cite relevant prior work that supports the importance of conformation in CK1 phosphorylation and provides disease relevance.

results.result: Prior work showed that EI peptides alone cannot be phosphorylated and that S828 is critical in cells and C. elegans, which the current study extends by showing full-length hAgo2 with guide and specific target is required.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75 and C117 accurately cite prior work and show how the current findings (C72) extend and refine previous understanding.

results.result: Prior work showed EI phosphorylation doesn't affect GW182 interaction, cofactors aren't required for phosphorylation, PP6 knockout decreases RISC-mRNA binding, and the phosphorylation cycling process itself is important.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C80 cite relevant prior work and integrate it with current findings (C77 based on current data). These provide important context for the mechanism.

results.result: The authors speculate that phosphorylation occurs after target repression is established, and that multiple phosphorylations ensure time for repression initiation before target release.
results.evaluation: Claims C82 and C83 are explicitly speculative and not directly tested. While reasonable hypotheses based on prior in vivo findings, they require temporal dynamics studies to validate.

results.result: GW182 tethering can bypass RISC, siRNA slicing promotes target release by destabilizing the duplex, and TDMD targets with extended 3' pairing don't need phosphorylation-promoted release.
results.evaluation: Claims C84, C86-C88 cite appropriate prior work and integrate it with current findings (C87) to explain why different target types behave differently.

results.result: The ZT1 target corresponds to a natural miR-200 binding site in ZEB1's 3' UTR, was identified as sensitive to EI phosphorylation in prior eCLIP experiments, and is functionally relevant for epithelial-mesenchymal transitions.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99 are supported by appropriate citations and justify the choice of experimental system.
